artifacts.title: Three questions worth publishing.
artifacts.introduction: Each content theme gives the owner something useful to consider before a sales conversation.

items.label: Theme 01 / Readiness
items.title: Are you ready to grow, or already stretched?
items.body: Article outline: name the opportunity; review capacity, ownership, and cash requirements; identify what must be in place; end with one readiness question for the owner.

items.label: Theme 02 / Tradeoffs
items.title: What will you stop doing to make room?
items.body: Social series: one post on competing priorities, one on the cost of maintaining them all, and one on choosing a decision criterion before evaluating options.

items.label: Theme 03 / Next steps
items.title: What can you learn before committing?
items.body: A short checklist on the assumptions to test, the information to gather, and the person responsible for the next decision.

artifacts.title: A sample post, ready to read.
artifacts.introduction: Writing example for a professional-services company page.

items.label: Social post
items.title: Before adding a new growth priority, name the tradeoff.
items.body: A new market, a new service, and a new hire can all sound like the next right move. The question is whether the business can support them at the same time. Before committing, write down three things: what this move is meant to change, what it will require from the business, and what you will pause to make room. If those answers are still vague, the next step may be a better brief rather than a bigger plan. What decision would become easier if the tradeoff were explicit?

faqs.question: Do we need all three services?
faqs.answer: No. Start with the work that solves your immediate problem. If your positioning is already clear, you can begin with Content Studio or Demand Campaigns. We can review fit together before agreeing a scope.

faqs.question: Is advertising spend included?
faqs.answer: No. Demand Campaigns is a management fee. Your media budget is additional and paid through your advertising account. The package covers up to $10,000 in monthly media spend; larger budgets need a separate scope.

faqs.question: Does Content Studio include design or video?
faqs.answer: The listed package is writing-only. Graphics, photography, video, community management, and email distribution or automation are separately scoped.

faqs.question: How long is the engagement?
faqs.answer: Brand Blueprint is a project, usually taking about 2–3 weeks after inputs and interviews. Our proposed retainer terms start with 90 days, then continue monthly with 30 days' notice. Your written agreement confirms the final terms.

faqs.question: Who owns the accounts and work?
faqs.answer: Your business owns its advertising accounts and data. Ownership and transfer of deliverables follow the written agreement. We do not guarantee a number of leads, sales, or revenue.

guides.title: What to clarify before spending on ads.
guides.summary: Six questions that turn “we should run ads” into a usable campaign brief.
guides.introduction: An advertising budget is easier to use well when the business decisions around it are made first. Before choosing an audience or writing an ad, work through the offer, destination, and follow-up together. The answers do not need to fill a long document. They need to be specific enough to guide the campaign.

sections.heading: Start with one offer and one action.
paragraphs: “Promote the business” leaves too many decisions open. Choose the service, product, or introductory offer the campaign will focus on, then name the action you want someone to take. A quote request and a purchase need different messages, destinations, and follow-up.
Write a sentence that names the offer, intended audience, and next step. If several audiences or offers compete for the same sentence, choose the first priority before expanding the brief.

sections.heading: Define who can actually use the offer.
paragraphs: Describe the customer’s situation, need, and ability to take the next step. Include the market you can serve and any practical limits. For a local service, location matters. For a B2B offer, the buyer’s business problem and role may matter more than a broad industry label.
Treat this as a starting hypothesis. The campaign should help you learn whether the offer and message reach suitable people.

sections.heading: Check the destination before buying the visit.
paragraphs: Read the destination as someone seeing the offer for the first time. Can they understand what is included, whether it fits them, and what happens next? Test the form, checkout, or booking route on a phone as well as a larger screen.
If the destination needs development, creative production, or substantial tracking work, identify that scope before launch. An ad management fee does not automatically cover those tasks.

sections.heading: Separate the budgets and define the evidence.
paragraphs: List the agency fee, launch or onboarding cost, media budget, and any production or technical costs separately. Then agree what you can measure reliably. A calendar click is different from a completed booking, and a submitted inquiry still needs to be assessed for fit.
Establish the starting position and a review window before making changes. Evaluate results in the context of spend, the buying cycle, and the volume of useful actions.

sections.heading: Give the next step an owner.
paragraphs: Decide who receives an inquiry, who follows up, and who approves campaign changes. A campaign brief should describe what the business will do after the click as clearly as what the ad will say.
list: Offer: what exactly are we promoting?
Audience: who needs it, and where can we serve them?
Action: what should they do next?
Destination: is that action working?
Budget and measurement: what is separate, and what counts?
Ownership: who approves, responds, and reviews?

guides.title: How one expert interview becomes a month of content.
guides.summary: A worked example of turning a business conversation into themes, post ideas, and an article.
guides.introduction: Useful content often starts with the questions a business answers every week. An interview gives those answers a structure. The writing work is to find the specific insight, explain it in the company’s voice, and give each piece a purpose. Here is an original fictional example using Northline Advisory.

sections.heading: Ask about decisions, not just topics.
paragraphs: A question such as “What should we post about growth?” usually produces a list of broad themes. More useful prompts ask what customers are deciding, what they misunderstand, and what information changes the conversation.

For the fictional Northline interview, the central prompt is: “What do owners overlook before adding another growth priority?” The sample answer is: “They discuss the new opportunity before deciding what the business can stop doing to make room.” This is an invented source excerpt for the demonstration.

sections.heading: Find the idea that can support several pieces.
paragraphs: The useful idea is the tradeoff behind a growth decision. It can support a short explanation, a practical question, a checklist, and a longer article without repeating the same paragraph.
Keep a source note for each angle so the writer and reviewer can trace the idea back to the conversation. Check the meaning with the expert before adding claims or examples they did not provide.
list: Readiness: is the business able to support the new priority?
Tradeoffs: what must pause to make room?
Next steps: what can the owner learn before committing?

sections.heading: Give each post a different job.
paragraphs: An eight-post writing plan can combine explanation, practical prompts, and a route to a deeper article. The format should follow the point, rather than forcing every post into the same template. This sample plan demonstrates the structure; it is not a completed monthly delivery.
list: 1. Explain why every new priority creates a tradeoff.
2. Ask what the business would pause to make room.
3. Share a three-question readiness checklist.
4. Explain the difference between an opportunity and a priority.
5. Describe an assumption an owner can test first.
6. Answer a common objection to narrowing the plan.
7. Introduce the longer article with its most useful question.
8. Invite readers to review one decision using the checklist.

sections.heading: Build one article around the full explanation.
paragraphs: A proposed article, “Before your next growth move, name the tradeoff,” can expand the same idea: describe the competing priorities, explain the capacity question, work through a fictional example, and end with a short decision checklist.
This gives the article a different purpose from the posts. It develops the reasoning and provides a useful resource to link to when the same question comes up again.

sections.heading: Review the batch before publishing.
paragraphs: Check accuracy, voice, examples, and the action each piece asks the reader to take. Collect feedback through one approval route so the writing can be revised consistently.

Content Studio includes a monthly source interview, eight written social posts for one profile or page, and one article up to 1,200 words or one email up to 800 words. The editorial calendar and review cycle connect those pieces. Graphics, community management, and email distribution are separately scoped.

guides.title: Brand strategy or a new logo: what does your business need?
guides.summary: Identify whether the problem is the message, the visual identity, or both before commissioning the work.
guides.introduction: A new logo can change how a business looks. Positioning changes how the business explains its offer and why someone should choose it. Both can matter, but they solve different parts of the problem. Start by identifying what your customers and your own team are struggling to understand.

sections.heading: Look for the question behind the request.
paragraphs: “We need a refresh” might mean the visuals feel dated. It might also mean the offer has changed, the company is serving a different audience, or every sales conversation starts with a long explanation.
Write down what should become easier after the work. If the answer is “people should understand what we do and who it is for,” positioning and messaging deserve attention before visual execution.

sections.heading: Check whether the offer is easy to explain.
paragraphs: Ask a few people close to the business to describe the priority customer, the problem you solve, and the reason to choose your offer. Differences can reveal decisions that a logo brief alone cannot settle.
A useful strategy brings those decisions together in a positioning statement, value proposition, message hierarchy, and voice guidance. These give later writing and design work a shared direction.
list: Who are we prioritizing?
What are they trying to decide or achieve?
What do we offer them?
Which reasons to believe can we actually support?
What should we emphasize first?

sections.heading: Assess the visual system on its own terms.
paragraphs: If the message is settled but the identity is inconsistent, hard to use, or poorly suited to the business, visual identity work may be the next need. That could involve a logo, typography, colors, photography, or application guidelines.
Write those requirements into a separate design brief. A strategy document can inform visual decisions, but the strategy deliverable and the identity production should each have an explicit scope.

sections.heading: Connect the decisions to the next 90 days.
paragraphs: A positioning exercise is more useful when the business knows where the message will appear next. Choose the service introduction, content themes, and campaign brief that need attention first.

For example, the fictional Northline concept starts with the owner’s growth decision, then uses that positioning to shape a headline and content themes. The sample shows how the reasoning informs the writing. It does not represent a completed client engagement.

sections.heading: Choose a scope that matches the problem.
paragraphs: Brand Blueprint covers stakeholder input, a competitor review, one priority buyer profile, positioning, voice guidance, three content themes, and a 90-day plan. Logo and visual identity design, naming, photography, video, and website development are separately scoped.
Bring your existing materials and the decisions you need to make. The first conversation should help establish which work is useful now and which work depends on it.
